title: arXiv AI — Friday, 6 November 2026: five notable papers
global_caveat: arXiv has no official trending chart; ordering is inferred from corroborating public discussion and paper-specific signals. Citation evidence is limited for papers this new, and the selection is curated and non-exhaustive because the broad machine-readable candidate query did not return.

sections.title: The Last Mile to the Real World: Agent-Native Primitives as Reusable Building Blocks for Solving Real-World Tasks
sections.abstract: The authors introduce agent-native primitives and HEELO, which composes, verifies, and improves task-specific agent harnesses; they report gains across 20+ benchmarks and 46 tasks on their real-world platform.
sections.claimed_contribution: The paper describes HEELO as a framework that assembles reusable, resource-specific agent primitives into task graphs and revises them against environmental evidence.
sections.unique_caveat: The abstract's real-world results include 46 tasks on the authors' heelo.dev platform; that evaluation does not establish performance across arbitrary live deployments.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: Broad AI cross-listing plus same-day coverage in multiple independent research digests and a separate technical explainer; this is evidence of discussion, not a readership count.

sections.title: Scientist World: Grow a Research World for AI-Scientists
sections.abstract: The paper turns research papers into executable environments, releasing 1,000 verified tasks and reporting results for AI agents that improve or innovate methods within them.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors report an automated pipeline that reproduces papers as runnable baselines and creates 1,000 independently verified research environments, with recorded agent research traces.
sections.unique_caveat: The headline leaderboard is based on ten lower-compute environments; a positive result is relative to a reproduced method on selected tasks, not a general measure of scientific ability.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: Cross-listed across three core AI categories and independently discussed by several research roundups; these provide corroboration of attention, not a measured popularity metric.

sections.title: The Memory Trap: Language Agents Overgeneralize from Benign Interactions
sections.abstract: Across six frontier models and constructed tasks, the authors find that benign persistent memories can generalize beyond their original scope and lead to unsafe actions, biased judgments, or weakened tests.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors identify two routes to memory traps—overgeneralization while writing a memory and overgeneralization when acting on it—and test consequences across autonomy, feedback, and coding scenarios.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors frame the results as susceptibility tests, not estimates of real-world frequency; scenarios are scripted or constructed, and most tested models come from one model family.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: Three core-category cross-lists and substantial independent technical discussion from a detailed daily briefing and agent research digest.

sections.title: MCPHallu: Benchmarking Reasoning, Execution, and Memory Hallucinations in MCP Agents
sections.abstract: MCPHallu evaluates 14 agents on 358 tasks across 36 production MCP servers, separating four failure types and finding the lowest average scores on tasks with unreachable goals.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors introduce structurally triggered tasks for diagnosing Branch Collapse, Unreachable Goal, Tool Misuse, and Context Forgetting in MCP trajectories.
sections.unique_caveat: The reported results are bounded by this 358-task benchmark, its 36 isolated server environments, and the tested 14-agent cohort; they do not estimate failure rates across deployed MCP use.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: Listed as a NeurIPS 2026 poster and covered by an independent daily benchmark source; the multi-server benchmark makes it directly relevant to the agent-systems cluster.

sections.title: QRAE: Query-Relevant Attention Entropy for Context Compression in DeepSearch Agents
sections.abstract: QRAE uses selected attention heads to keep likely useful retrieved chunks in an agent's reasoning context while caching uncertain chunks for later reconsideration; the authors report lower token use and latency with a modest task-success increase.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors propose query-relevant attention entropy as a prefill-based signal for admitting retrieved evidence chunks without an extra generative compression pass.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors identify evidence that cannot be localized to retrieved text as future work; generalization to those tasks remains untested.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: Public research-tracker coverage, inclusion in a daily agent research radar, and evaluation spanning multiple model–benchmark settings; it ranks below more broadly discussed, cross-listed papers.
